<meta>continues from previous page: ...The gods themselves give warning and command that He be worshipped everywhere. But the unlearned and those of impious nature, to whom fate has not truly granted the reception of gifts from the gods, nor the understanding of the immortal Jupiter, do not heed both the gods and divine men; they have rejected all the gods indeed, but they have chosen not only to follow no hatreds toward the forbidden demons, but even to revere them. Yet, while pretending to worship God, they do not perform the very things through which God is adored. For God, as the Father of all, is in need of nothing; but it is well for us when we adore Him through justice, chastity, and other virtues, making our very life a prayer to Him through imitation and the inquiry of Him. For inquiry, he says, purges; imitation deifies by working an affection toward Him. He has indeed preached well that God is the Father and has spoken of the virtues by which He must be worshipped. The prophetic books of the Hebrews are full of these precepts, whether the life of the holy is praised or blamed. But it was only in Christians—or rather, it is slandered as much as the demons, whom he deems gods, desire—as if it were difficult for anyone to recall what base things and what dishonors were performed in the theaters and temples for the sake of the gods, and to attend to what is read, said, and heard in the churches, or what is offered to the true God, and from this to understand where there is an edifice and where a ruin of morals. Who, moreover, told this to him or inspired him, if not a diabolical spirit, such a vain and open lie: that Christians revere rather than hate the demons whom the Hebrews were forbidden to worship? But that God whom the wise men of the Hebrews worshipped also forbids sacrificing to the celestial, holy angels and virtues of God—whom we venerate and love as most blessed fellow citizens in this mortal pilgrimage of ours—thundering in His law which He gave to His Hebrew people; and He brought it in very menacingly, saying: "He who sacrifices to the gods will be eradicated." And lest anyone should think it was commanded that one should not sacrifice to the wicked, earthly spirits—whom this man calls the "least" or "lesser"—because they are also called gods in the holy scriptures, they are not [called gods] of the Hebrews

<column-break/>

but of the nations, which the seventy translators <note>The Septuagint</note> clearly placed in the Psalm, saying: "For all the gods of the nations are demons." Lest anyone, therefore, think that while it is forbidden to sacrifice to these demons, it is permitted to sacrifice to the celestial ones—either to all or to some—He immediately added: "Except to the Lord alone," that is, except to the Lord only, lest by chance someone think that the "Lord alone" refers to the sun god, to whom he thinks sacrifice should be made. That this is not to be understood in this way is very easily found in the Greek scriptures. Therefore, the God of the Hebrews, to whom such a great man and even this philosopher bears witness, gave a law to His Hebrew people, written in the Hebrew language—not obscure and unknown, but now spread among all nations—in which law it is written: "He who sacrifices to the gods will be eradicated, unless to the Lord only." What need is there in this law of His and in His prophets to investigate many things about this matter? Or rather, not to investigate, for they are not abstruse or rare, but to collect the open and frequent ones, and to place them in this my disputation, by which it appears clearer than light that the true and supreme God wished to be sacrificed to by no one at all except Himself alone. Behold, let this one thing, briefly—or rather, grandly and menacingly, but truthfully—spoken by that God whom their most learned men so excellently preach, be heard, be feared, be fulfilled, lest eradication follow the disobedient. "He who sacrifices to the gods will be eradicated," He says, "except to the Lord alone." Not that He is in need of any thing, but because it is profitable for us that we be His. For it is sung to Him in the sacred writings of the Hebrews: "I said to the Lord, You are my God, for You do not need my goods." The most illustrious and best sacrifice to Him, however, is ourselves. This is His city, the mystery of which we celebrate with our oblations, which are known to the faithful, just as we have argued in the preceding books. For the oracles thundered through the Hebrew prophets that the victims which the Jews offered in the shadow of things to come were going to cease, and that the nations would offer one sacrifice from the rising of the sun to the setting, just as we now see happening.

<summary>Augustine argues that the Hebrew law, widely known and clear, forbids sacrifice to any but the one true God, refuting the idea that sacrifices to lesser spirits or celestial beings were ever permitted. He defines the true sacrifice as the self-offering of the faithful, which constitutes the City of God.</summary>
<keywords>Sacrifice, Hebrews, Demonology, Idolatry, Law of Moses, Christian worship, City of God, Porphyry</keywords>
